As a freshman playing [[college basketball]] with the [[UCLA Bruins men's basketball|UCLA Bruins]], he earned second-team [[List of All-Pac-12 Conference men's basketball teams|all-conference]] honors in the [[Pac-12 Conference men's basketball|Pac-12]] in 2015. After the season, Looney decided to forgo his college eligibility and enter the [[2015 NBA draft]], and was selected in the first round by the [[Golden State Warriors]] with the 30th overall pick. He won three [[NBA championship]]s during his 10-year tenure with the Warriors. Growing up in [[Wisconsin]], Looney was named the top high school player in the state as a senior in 2014. He also received national recognition as a five-star prospect and earned [[All-American]] honors. In his only season at UCLA, Looney led all freshmen in the nation in [[double-double]]s, recording double figures in both [[point (basketball)|points]] and [[rebound (basketball)|rebounds]] in 15 games. One of the top players in the Pac-12, he was also named to their all-freshman team. As a rookie with Golden State, Looney's playing time was limited after undergoing surgery on both his hips. The next season, a strained left hip sidelined him for most of the [[NBA playoffs|playoffs]] during their championship run. Finally healthy in 2017–18, Looney became a regular in the Warriors' rotation as an undersized [[Center (basketball)|center]], helping them win a second straight championship. Looney won a third championship with Golden State in 2022 as their starting center. After ten seasons with the Warriors, Looney signed with the [[New Orleans Pelicans]] in 2025. ==Early life== Looney was born in [[Milwaukee]], [[Wisconsin]], to Doug and Victoria Looney.{{cite web|url=http://www.uclabruins.com/ViewArticle.dbml?DB_OEM_ID=30500&ATCLID=209575061|title=Kevon Looney Bio|work=UCLABruins.com|access-date=November 21, 2014}} Growing up, he was coached by his father, who played as a [[forward (basketball)|forward]] at [[Schreiner University]] in [[Kerrville, Texas]], and became the school's career [[rebound (basketball)|rebounding]] leader. Looney also watched his brother Kevin, who was six years older, play [[pickup game]]s. Like his brother, Looney became a [[Los Angeles Lakers]] and [[Kobe Bryant]] fan, and watched tapes of Bryant, copying his moves. His brother would let him play basketball with him, but only if Kevon rebounded more and shot less. Capable of handling the ball, creating his own shot, and shooting,{{cite news|last=Thompson II|first=Marcus|title=Thompson: A mother's faith has long fueled Kevon Looney's self-belief|date=January 3, 2019|work=The Athletic|url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/747202/2019/01/03/thompson-a-mothers-faith-has-long-fueled-kevon-looneys-self-belief/|url-access=subscription|access-date=June 6, 2019}} [[mixtape]]s on [[YouTube]] hailed Looney as "the next KD", in reference to future [[Golden State Warriors|Golden State]] teammate [[Kevin Durant]]. Hamilton went undefeated in conference play to win its first league title in four years, and Looney earned his second City Conference player of the year award.{{cite news|first=Mark |last=Stewart |url=http://www.jsonline.com/sports/preps/milwaukee-hamiltons-looney-brown-deers-appleby-win-state-honors-b99233979z1-252571871.html |title=Milwaukee Hamilton's Looney, Brown Deer's Appleby win state honors |work=JSOnline.com |publisher=The Milwaukee Journal Sentinel |date=March 26, 2014 |access-date=March 26, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141129044635/http://www.jsonline.com/sports/preps/milwaukee-hamiltons-looney-brown-deers-appleby-win-state-honors-b99233979z1-252571871.html |archive-date=November 29, 2014 |url-status=live}} Looney gained national recognition, becoming just the second player in [[Milwaukee Public Schools]] history, and the sixth ever in Wisconsin, to be named a [[McDonald's All-American Game|McDonald's All-American]]; he was also a [[Parade All-America Boys Basketball Team|''Parade'' All-American]]. Looney was named [[Wisconsin Mr. Basketball]] by the Wisconsin Basketball Coaches Association, and both [[Gatorade Player of the Year awards|Gatorade]] and the [[Associated Press]] named him their state player of the year.{{cite news|first=Mark |last=Stewart |url=http://www.jsonline.com/sports/preps/hamiltons-kevon-looney-not-resting-on-laurels-b99245340z1-254846611.html |title=Hamilton's Kevon Looney not resting on laurels |work=JSOnline.com |publisher=The Milwaukee Journal Sentinel |date=April 10, 2014 |access-date=April 10, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141129044529/http://www.jsonline.com/sports/preps/hamiltons-kevon-looney-not-resting-on-laurels-b99245340z1-254846611.html |archive-date=November 29, 2014 |url-status=live}} Looney was listed as a five-star prospect by [[Rivals.com]], [[ESPN]].com and [[Scout.com]], who ranked him nationally as the No. 10, No. 12, and No. 15 player, respectively. [[File:Kevon Looney and Malik Martin.jpg|thumb|upright|Looney as a UCLA freshman on defense against [[USC Trojans men's basketball|USC]]]] Upon his arrival at UCLA over the summer before his freshman season, Looney suffered a hip injury while playing in the gym. Bruins guard [[Isaac Hamilton]] shot the ball and fell into the right leg of Looney, who was positioning to rebound the ball. He rested for two to three weeks before the season. Looney did not miss a practice or game all year, but the injury hampered his lateral movement and speed. Looney avoided changing directions, and played more like a lumbering big man. Playing [[Power forward (basketball)|power forward]] for the Bruins, he was one of the top freshmen in the country in [[2014–15 UCLA Bruins men's basketball team|2014–15]].{{cite news|first=Zach |last=Helfand |url=http://www.latimes.com/sports/ucla/la-sp-ucla-looney-lakers-20150312-story.html |title=UCLA's Kevon Looney is on the bubble too |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=March 11, 2015 |access-date=March 13, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150314052548/http://www.latimes.com/sports/ucla/la-sp-ucla-looney-lakers-20150312-story.html |archive-date=March 14, 2015 |url-status=live}} During the season opener, Looney debuted with 20 points, nine rebounds, and three assists in a 113–78 win over [[Montana State Bobcats men's basketball|Montana State]]. [[CBS Sports]] called his performance "one of the more impressive freshman debuts in UCLA's rich history." Looney was limited to playing in just 20 games during the season, averaging only 3.4 points and 3.3 rebounds per game.{{cite news|first=Dalton|last=Johnson|title=How Looney reacted to offseason Warriors trade rumors|date=December 24, 2020|website=NBCSports.com|url=https://www.nbcsports.com/bayarea/warriors/how-kevon-looney-reacted-multiple-warriors-offseason-trade-rumors|access-date=December 31, 2020}} On May 19, 2020, Looney underwent surgery to repair a core muscle injury and was expected to be ready for the start of the following season.{{cite web|title=Kevon Looney Undergoes Successful Surgery|url=https://www.nba.com/warriors/news/looney-surgery-20200520|date=May 20, 2020|website=NBA.com|access-date=May 20, 2020}} Looney began the [[2020–21 Golden State Warriors season|2020–21 season]] as a backup to rookie center [[James Wiseman]], the No. 2 overall draft pick.{{cite news|first=Alex|last=Didion|title=Looney praises Warriors rookie Wiseman's 'feel for game'|date=December 26, 2020|website=NBCSports.com|url=https://www.nbcsports.com/bayarea/warriors/warriors-kevon-looney-praises-james-wisemans-feel-game-rookie|access-date=December 31, 2020}} However, Looney became the Warriors' only true center after the rookie suffered a meniscus tear and was sidelined for the season. Looney is most suited to playing power forward.{{cite news|last=Kroichick|first=Ron|title=Kevon Looney's big first half goes for naught in Warriors loss|date=January 4, 2019|newspaper=San Francisco [[wingspan]], he is also a capable, [[small ball (basketball)|small-ball]] center who is able to guard all five [[Basketball positions|positions]]. Looney's length allows him to switch assignments and defend guards. He moves fairly well on the perimeter,{{cite news|last=Vecenie|first=Sam|title=The Top 75 NBA free agents you need to know|date=June 29, 2018|work=The Athletic|url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/411254/2018/06/29/vecenie-the-top-75-nba-free-agents-you-need-to-know/|quote=Over the course of his fourth season, he proved himself valuable to the Warriors as a switchable defender who could move reasonably well out on the perimeter in their scheme.|url-access=subscription}} and is not easily lured by [[pump fake]]s. Looney can also defend the rim. Looney had limited mobility after his hip surgeries. Lacking explosion, he worked on faking opponents and getting his defender off balance. After becoming healthier and losing weight, Looney became more athletic and proficient at catching lob passes. During the summer 2018 off-season, he worked on finishing the lobs without having to land first. Looney practiced in a Shoot 360 facility in Oakland, which gives players feedback in real time on their technique. He said: "I like to get the feedback. How did I shoot today?
